title: The middle of three takes all
hook: Two people split $1 evenly. Add a third who can only deal with one of them. Now what?

doesNotKnow: that the person with a spare partner can push the split almost all the way to themselves

misconception: Two people bargaining over $1 split it about evenly, whoever else is around.
objective: The learner can explain that on a line of three, whichever end the centre leaves out will offer to take less, so the ends bid each other down until the centre has the whole $1 (in the limit), the only stable split.

claims.text: On the stage, each round the end Bo left out offers to take 10 cents less and Bo switches, so the asks fall from $0.50 to $0.00 in five rounds and Bo's share rises to the whole $1.
claims.source: Lesson rule (10-cent undercut). Demo.tsx round(k): Bo's share 0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9, 1.0; re-run in node (ncm-e00).

claims.text: On a line of three where the centre can deal with only one end, the only stable outcome (no one can undercut, and no pair could both do better by dealing together) gives the centre the whole $1, in the limit; the centre's power comes from the spare partner, not from bargaining skill.
claims.source: An unmatched end gets 0, so it would accept any positive share; the matched end's share must be 0 or the left-out end can offer Bo more. Brief check: {centre: 1, endMatched: 0}. Easley and Kleinberg 2010, ch. 12 (stability).

claims.text: In this model two people with no one else to turn to split the $1 evenly.
claims.source: Lesson rule (symmetric split with equal, zero outside options). Stage message 'No one else to turn to: they split evenly.'

claims.text: The lesson is a simplified model: one deal per person, 10-cent undercuts, two people alone split evenly.
claims.source: Assumptions of Demo.tsx; stage chip 'Model: each person makes one deal' and the reveal's last line.

recall.question: Dee can split $1 with Eli or with Fay, but only one of them; Eli and Fay have no one else. In a stable outcome, what does Dee get?
recall.why: Whoever Dee leaves out gets nothing, so they offer to take less; the two bid each other down until Dee has (nearly) the whole $1.
